title: AI Photo Trends Right Now: What People Are Posting in 2026
h1: AI Photo Trends Right Now: What People Are Posting and How to Try Each
description: A dated list of the AI photo trends named in roundups this month, who reported each one, which you can try on one photo, and how to tell a trend from a meme.
summary: No single AI photo trend is on top this week, and we found no source that ranks them with real numbers. Roundups dated November 20 to 25, 2026 name GTA 6 loading-screen portraits, black-and-white sweater portraits, chibi characters, three-frame snow pictures and Christmas flash and photo booth looks, on top of the boxed action figures and 80s and 2000s camera snapshots that have come back since September. This page lists what named sources report, with dates, and which of them you can try on your own photo.

sections.heading: New in roundups this week (November 20 to 25, 2026)
paragraphs: This page was checked on November 25, 2026. Every row below comes from a named page and the date shown on it, newest report first. None of those pages gives counts of how many people posted a trend, so read “popular” here as “covered in roundups”, not as a ranking.

sections.heading: Which ones last and which are one-week memes
paragraphs: The sources disagree on how fast trends move. SocialThink wrote on September 14, 2026 that some trends last for weeks and others disappear almost as quickly as they arrive, and Nano Potato wrote on November 24, 2026 that one look fills TikTok for two weeks before the next one takes over. Kenerate AI, in a guide updated on November 25, 2026, still says it found no reliable source showing which single look is peaking this month.

Two looks have a longer record. Quantslant describes the boxed action figure in two waves, the first in April 2025 and the second in September 2025, and says that in 2026 the format became a template people repeat with each new image model. It calls this a steady, seasonally refreshed trend, which is its own assessment and not a measurement. ImgCruncher still lists toy figures as the longest-running trend of the year on November 25, 2026. Chibi shows a similar pattern: Moneycontrol reported it as one of the biggest visual trends on Instagram on May 12, 2026, and three guides were still covering it in November.

The newest wave is the opposite case. ClipVersus says template sites trace the earliest sweater portrait post with the full prompt to November 9, 2026, and notes that no post had reached a million plays by November 12. Our reading of all the sources is that toy-style figures, cartoon avatars and old-camera looks keep coming back in new forms, while a style tied to one tool, one game launch or one week's prompt tends to fade.

sections.heading: How to judge a trend claim
items: Look for a date. A roundup from the spring cannot tell you what people are posting in November.
Look for a named source. “Going viral” with no link or name behind it is a guess.
Look for numbers. Without counts of posts or views, “most popular” only means the author saw it a lot.
Note who is writing. Many roundups, including this one, come from sites that offer an AI photo tool, so a trend that fits the author's product deserves a second source.

Check whether the trend is a style or a character. A style such as grain, flash, clay or felt can be recreated by anyone. A look that depends on a film character or a studio's art style is a different matter, and PiCraft does not make those. A game's mood can be described without its art, which is what the neon city poster does.

sections.heading: What nearly every trend has in common
paragraphs: The how-to pages from PromptUp, Kenerate AI, PromptLike and Quantslant describe nearly the same recipe, whatever the trend is called. PromptLike and Quantslant both trace most failed results to the photo or to asking for too much at once: a dark, blurry or side-facing photo, or a prompt that changes the outfit, the background and the hairstyle together.
items: Upload one sharp photo with the face or the pet clearly visible, in even light.
Say what must stay the same, usually the face, hairstyle and skin tone.
Name the light, the camera or the material that makes the look, such as direct flash, film grain or modelling clay.
Give the shape you need, such as vertical 9:16 for Stories or 4:5 for a feed post.
Make two or three versions and keep the one that still looks like you.

sections.heading: Three ways to try a trend on your own photo
paragraphs: In ChatGPT or Gemini, with a prompt. Upload your photo, paste the text and make a few versions. Many look pages on PiCraft carry a prompt you can copy, for example the one on the [80s Flashback page](/create/photo-trend-maker/80s-flashback), the one on the [Y2K Digital Camera page](/create/photo-trend-maker/y2k-digicam) and the one on the [Chibi Character page](/create/photo-trend-maker/chibi-character). A prompt can give a different result in each chat tool, so treat it as a starting point.

On PiCraft, in one click. The [Photo Trend Maker](/create/photo-trend-maker) has 35 looks. You upload one photo, choose a look and a size, and download a finished JPG at the exact pixel size. There is no prompt to write. New visitors get free credits and do not need an account, and one credit makes one picture.

With your own wording, in Image to Image. [Image to Image](/image-to-image) lets you write the changes yourself and add reference photos. Use it for a trend that has no ready-made look, such as a Lofi Dusk portrait or a Polaroid-style print, or when you want to pick the sweater color yourself.

sections.heading: Trends PiCraft does not make
paragraphs: Some trends depend on a named film character, a brand's packaging, a studio's art style or a real public figure. PiCraft has no looks for these. The biggest trend this week, the GTA 6 loading-screen portrait, is the borderline case. The [Neon City Game Poster](/create/photo-trend-maker/neon-city-game-poster) paints the same kind of picture, a neon sunset, palm trees and a sports car, from a generic description, and uses no game artwork, characters, logos or title. It is not affiliated with any game or its publisher. The other looks on the [photo trends page](/categories/photo-trends) copy cameras, materials, objects and generic art styles such as chibi, which anyone can describe without borrowing someone else's work.

The Terms say to upload only photos you took or have the right to use, that every recognizable person must have agreed, and not to upload photos of children. Read the text a result draws into the picture, such as a date stamp or a headline, before you post it, because AI can misspell words.

faq.q: What is the AI photo trend right now?
faq.a: There is no single one. Roundups dated November 20 to 25, 2026 name GTA 6 loading-screen portraits, black-and-white sweater portraits, chibi characters, three-frame snow pictures and Christmas photo booth and party flash looks, while boxed action figures and 80s and 2000s camera snapshots keep returning. The tables on this page show who reported each one and when.

faq.q: How long do AI photo trends last?
faq.a: It varies. SocialThink wrote in September 2026 that some last for weeks and others fade almost at once. Quantslant describes the boxed action figure as returning in waves since April 2025, and Moneycontrol was already reporting chibi pictures as a big Instagram trend in May 2026, six months before the November guides.

faq.q: Which AI photo trend is the most popular?
faq.a: We found no source that ranks them with real numbers, so we do not name one. A roundup that calls a trend the most popular without counts of posts or views is giving an impression, not a measurement.

faq.q: Can I make the GTA 6 photo trend on PiCraft?
faq.a: A version of it, yes. The [Neon City Game Poster](/create/photo-trend-maker/neon-city-game-poster) paints you as the lead of an imaginary city game with a neon sunset, palm trees and a sports car. It is a generic painted poster that uses no game artwork, characters, logos or title, and it is not affiliated with the game or its publisher. The roundups name ChatGPT and Gemini as the tools people use for the original.

faq.q: Can I do an AI photo trend for free?
faq.a: Often, yes. Quantslant reports that Gemini and ChatGPT both allow a limited number of free images, and that the limits have changed before. On PiCraft, new visitors get free credits and no account is needed.

faq.q: Do I need to write a prompt?
faq.a: In a chat image tool, yes, and the prompt matters. On PiCraft you pick a look and a size from a form, and the wording is already written. The look pages also show a prompt you can paste into another tool.

faq.q: Is it safe to upload my photo?
faq.a: Upload only photos you took or have the right to use, and only if everyone recognizable in them has agreed. Do not upload photos of children. Your photo on PiCraft is sent to our AI provider to make the image and is not shown to other visitors. The [Privacy Policy](/privacy) explains how long data is kept.
